757.title: Loi and the household
757.hook: Kabir's hymns speak to his wife, a reminder that saints lived in homes
757.howItsDone: Sikhs read Kabir's hymns, including those addressed to Loi, as part of Gurbani, and Sikh teaching holds up the householder's life, with work, family and shared food, as the setting for devotion.

segments.voice: Yesterday, jeevan mukat: dying to the ego while still alive, and so being free. Your line was free while living. Which small want did you let go of? Day seven hundred fifty-seven.

A pot of rice is on the fire. Someone has to buy thread tomorrow, and someone has to answer the knock at the door, because, tradition says, holy men kept turning up hungry. This is not a cave in the mountains. It's a weaver's house in a crowded city, with a family in it. And in a few of his hymns, the weaver turns from the crowd and speaks to one person by name: Loi. Today: Loi and the household.
screen: `A POT ON THE FIRE.` → `A KNOCK AT THE DOOR.` → `KABIR SPEAKS TO ONE PERSON.`

segments.voice: Many of Kabir's hymns in the Guru Granth Sahib close with the words kahat kabir sunahu re loi. Most translators hear loi there as people: Kabir says, listen, everyone. But in a few hymns Kabir speaks to Loi by name, and tradition says Loi was his wife. Sikh and Kabirpanthi tellings remember her as the woman who kept the house running while her husband sang, fed the visiting sadhus, and sometimes argued with him about the cost. So here is a saint whose world has a wife in it. Not as a temptation to run from. As someone he talks to. That matters because a popular picture of holiness says you leave home to find God. The ascetic walks away from the kitchen, the market and the marriage bed. Kabir's hymns quietly argue with that picture. He found the Lord at the loom, in a house with a family in it. Guru Nanak walked the same road. Sikh tradition remembers him as a householder: he married, raised a family, and in his later years at Kartarpur worked the fields, with a kitchen open to everyone. The Sikh word for that life is grihasti, the householder's life, and Sikh teaching holds it up as a place where a person can be fully devoted. Now notice what changes when the listener is at home. A crowd hears a saint once, at his best. The people who share his kitchen hear him every day, tired, late with the cloth. Say something holy to a crowd and they may clap. Say it to the person across the table and you'd better mean it. However you hear that closing word, as one woman's name or as everyone, the hymns are spoken to somebody, close enough to answer back. Holiness, here, is a conversation across the room.
screen: `KABIR SAYS, LISTEN.` · `LOI, BY NAME, IN A FEW HYMNS.` · `GURU NANAK LIVED AS A HOUSEHOLDER.` · `SAY IT AT HOME, AND MEAN IT.` · then, large: `SAINTS LIVE IN HOMES.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: say a kind word at home. First, the sit. Bring to mind the people you live with, or the person you last shared a meal with. See the ordinary room: the table, the shoes by the door. Let one of them come forward. Find one true, kind thing to say to them, small and specific. Thanks for the coffee. You handled that well. Hold the sentence for the rest of the sit, and plan when you'll say it. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out. The bell holds the time.
Loi and the household. The name Kabir speaks to in a few hymns, remembered as his wife, and the home where a saint lived and worked.
Your line: saints live in homes. Today, say your kind word out loud, at home, to the person it's meant for. Day seven hundred fifty-seven.

758.title: Dying at Maghar
758.hook: believing the holy city promised no special freedom, Kabir went to die at Maghar, a place thought unlucky (Kabir, Gauri)
758.howItsDone: Sikhs read Kabir's Maghar hymn as part of Gurbani, and Sikh teaching holds that liberation comes through the Name and grace, not through dying in a particular holy place.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Loi and the household: Kabir speaking his hymns across the room, at home. Your line was saints live in homes. Did your kind word get said? Day seven hundred fifty-eight.

Some places carry a promise. Pilgrims in Kabir's world believed that whoever died in Kashi, the holy city of Benares, would be set free. And there was another town, Maghar, with the opposite reputation: die there, people said, and your next birth would be a poor one. Kabir lived his whole life in Kashi. Then, near the end, by his own account in a hymn, he got up and went to Maghar. Today: dying at Maghar.
screen: `KASHI — THE CITY OF THE PROMISE.` → `MAGHAR — THE UNLUCKY TOWN.` → `KABIR GETS UP AND GOES.`

segments.voice: The hymn is in Raag Gauri, on Ang 326. Here's its turn, in paraphrase: my whole life I spent in Shiva's city, and at the time of death I rose and came to Maghar. Then Kabir asks the sharp question. If Kabir leaves his body in Kashi, what favor would he owe the Lord? If the city does the saving, the Lord has nothing left to do. Turn that over once. A promise tied to a place sounds generous, but it quietly moves freedom out of the heart and onto a map. Kabir refuses the trade. He'd rather owe everything to the Lord than owe it to an address. In another hymn he puts it flatly, in paraphrase: to one who has the Lord in the heart, Kashi and Maghar are the same. So the walk to Maghar isn't a stunt. It's the hymn acted out. Here's the second turn. Kabir doesn't mock the pilgrims. He doesn't say the holy city is bad. He says it isn't the thing that saves. That's a difference worth keeping. A place can be dear, can help you remember, can be full of people praying. Sikhs travel to historic gurdwaras, too. The Gurus taught that the bath that counts is in the Name, not only the water. And the third turn is about us. Some superstitions today are smaller: the lucky shirt, the seat always taken, the step never skipped. They can look harmless. Kabir's question still applies to them. If the shirt does the work, what's left for you, and what's left for God?
screen: `MY WHOLE LIFE IN SHIVA'S CITY.` · `WHAT FAVOR WOULD I OWE THE LORD?` · `KASHI AND MAGHAR, THE SAME.` · `THE LUCKY SHIRT, THE SAME QUESTION.` · then, large: `THE PLACE DOESN'T SAVE YOU.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: do one thing without superstition. First, the sit. Let your mind look for one small habit kept for luck, if you have one. The seat, the order of your morning, a number you avoid, a phrase before a test. If none comes, take any fixed habit. Just notice it, without scolding. Then choose: today, once, you'll do that thing the other way. Sit in a different chair. Skip the ritual. Feel what's left when the charm is gone. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out. The bell holds the time.
Dying at Maghar. Kabir leaving the holy city for the town thought unlucky, because the place doesn't do the saving.
Your line: the place doesn't save you. Today, do your one thing without the charm, and see that the day still holds. Day seven hundred fifty-eight.

759.title: Five saloks
759.hook: Kabir's couplets are short enough to carry in the pocket (ang 1364–1377)
759.howItsDone: Kabir's saloks are read and sung in gurdwaras with the rest of the Guru Granth Sahib, and many Sikhs learn favorite couplets by heart and quote them in conversation.

segments.voice: Yesterday, dying at Maghar: Kabir leaving the holy city, because the place doesn't save you. Which lucky habit did you skip, and did the day hold? Day seven hundred fifty-nine.

A sticky note on the fridge. A line written on the back of a hand before an exam. A phrase a grandmother said so often the whole family can finish it. Some words are built to travel light. Kabir's saloks are like that: short couplets, signed with his name at the start. They fill the pages of the Guru Granth Sahib from Ang 1364 to 1377. Today we take five of them out and turn each one over. Today: five saloks.
screen: `A STICKY NOTE ON THE FRIDGE.` → `TWO LINES, SIGNED KABIR.` → `FIVE TO CARRY.`

segments.voice: All five in paraphrase. The first is about time. Kabir, what you'd do tomorrow, do today; what you'd do today, do now. Later there'll be nothing to do, once death is standing over you. Short enough to say in the doorway, and it stings. The second is about this life. Kabir says a human birth is hard to come by, and it doesn't come again and again: like ripe fruit that falls in the forest, it never goes back onto the branch. One picture, and you can see it. The third is a little map. Where there is wisdom, there is dharma, right living. Where there is falsehood, there is sin. Where there is greed, there is death. And where there is forgiveness, there is the Lord himself. Notice where the line ends: not on a rule, but on forgiveness, with God standing in it. The fourth is a chain, told across several couplets. Kabir says, become a pebble on the path and drop your pride. Then he catches himself: a pebble still hurts a traveler's foot, so become dust. But dust blows up and soils the body, so become water. But water turns cold and hot, so become like the Lord. Each picture gets corrected by the next. It's humility that keeps checking itself. And the fifth, for the end of the day. Kabir, nothing in me is mine; whatever there is, is Yours. If I hand back to You what's Yours, what does it cost me? That's what a salok can do: take one ordinary thought and turn it until your grip loosens. They're built to be learned by heart, so they're there in the doorway when you need them.
screen: `DO IT TODAY; DO IT NOW.` · `RIPE FRUIT DOESN'T RETURN TO THE BRANCH.` · `WHERE FORGIVENESS IS, THE LORD IS.` · `PEBBLE, DUST, WATER, THE LORD.` · then, large: `NOTHING IN ME IS MINE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: read five saloks. You've just heard them. Now use the sit to keep one. Pick the salok that caught on something in you: do it now, the ripe fruit, forgiveness, the pebble, or nothing is mine. Say it to yourself slowly, in your own words. Then again. Let it get shorter each time, until it fits in one breath. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out. The bell holds the time.
Five saloks. Kabir's short couplets, signed with his name: do it now, the ripe fruit, forgiveness, the pebble, and nothing is mine.
Your line: short and sharp. Today, write your one salok on something you'll see, a note, a phone screen, and read it once at the moment it fits. Day seven hundred fifty-nine.

760.title: Kabir close
760.hook: a weaver who argued with priests and pirs and loved the Lord more than both
760.howItsDone: Kabir's hymns and saloks are part of the Guru Granth Sahib, sung in kirtan and read in gurdwaras alongside the Gurus' own words, and Sikhs honor him as a bhagat whose devotion the Gurus recognized.

segments.voice: Yesterday, five saloks: do it now, the ripe fruit, forgiveness, the pebble, nothing is mine. Your line was short and sharp. Which one did you carry? Day seven hundred sixty.

What do you call a man who tells a learned Brahmin to his face that birth makes no one higher, and then calls himself the Lord's dog? Fierce? Humble? Kabir's hymns won't let you pick one. He was a weaver of Benares who argued with the pandit on one side and the qazi on the other, and loved the Lord more than either argument. Today we lay the threads side by side. Today: Kabir close.
screen: `FIERCE? HUMBLE?` → `THE PANDIT AND THE QAZI.` → `THE THREADS SIDE BY SIDE.`

segments.voice: First, the weaver. Kabir worked the loom, a julaha, and he pictured the body and the whole world as cloth, warp and weft, with the Lord as the weaver. His mother wept that he sang instead of weaving; his answer was that the one Lord is the giver, for him and for the children too. Second, the arguments. In one hymn he says to the Brahmin, in paraphrase: you are a Brahmin and I'm a weaver of Kashi; try to understand my wisdom. In another he turns to the qazi and asks which book it is he's explaining. And he asked the man proud of high birth why he hadn't come into the world by some other road. But hear the other side of it too: he told both not to call the scriptures false. False, he said, is the one who doesn't reflect. The argument was never with the books. It was with pride wearing the books like a robe. Third, the love underneath. When he described himself, it wasn't as a champion. He was the worst of all, and everyone else was good. He was the Lord's dog, led on a chain. An elephant, in his hymn, bowed instead of charging. He spoke of dying to the ego while alive, and of going to Maghar because the place doesn't save you. He sang at home, to Loi. Lay those threads together and a pattern shows. Kabir's fierceness and his humility are the same cloth. He could be blunt with the powerful because he expected nothing from them, and humble before everyone else because he expected everything from the Lord. The Gurus kept his hymns in the Granth, and Sikhs sing them still. Tomorrow, a different voice: a Sufi of the Punjab.
screen: `A WEAVER, AND THE WORLD AS CLOTH.` · `TO THE BRAHMIN AND THE QAZI.` · `WORST OF ALL, THE LORD'S DOG.` · `FIERCE AND HUMBLE, ONE CLOTH.` · then, large: `WEAVE IT IN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: weave one kind act. In the sit, picture your day as cloth on a loom: the long threads already set, work, meals, errands, the people you'll pass. Now choose one cross-thread to pull through. One kind act, tucked into something you were doing anyway. Holding a door. Asking a real question. Clearing someone else's cup. Picture the exact moment it fits. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out. The bell holds the time.
Kabir close. The weaver of Benares: blunt with pride, humble before people, and devoted to the Lord, all in one cloth.
Your line: weave it in. Today, pull your one kind act through the day you already have, without making room for it. Day seven hundred sixty.

761.title: Sheikh Farid of Pakpattan
761.hook: Baba Farid, a Chishti Sufi of the twelfth and thirteenth centuries, whose Punjabi verses the Gurus treasured
761.howItsDone: Sheikh Farid's hymns and saloks are part of the Guru Granth Sahib and are sung in kirtan and read in gurdwaras with the rest of Gurbani; Farid is also honored by Muslims in the Punjab, and his shrine is in Pakpattan.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Kabir close: the weaver, fierce with pride and humble before the Lord. Your line was weave it in. Did your kind act find its thread? Day seven hundred sixty-one.

It's still dark. A man gets up, washes his hands, face and feet, and stands to pray before the light comes. Then he says something about himself, plainly, for anyone to hear: this path is hard, and I keep walking the world's way instead. That's the voice of Sheikh Farid, a Sufi, a Muslim mystic, of the Chishti order, whom tradition places at Pakpattan, in the Punjab, before the time of the Gurus. Today we meet him in his own words. Today: Sheikh Farid of Pakpattan.
screen: `STILL DARK. WASH, AND STAND.` → `THIS PATH IS HARD.` → `A SUFI IN THE PUNJAB.`

segments.voice: We met Farid in year one and saw how his verses came into the Guru's keeping. Today, listen to how he talks to himself. Farid's saloks in the Guru Granth Sahib often open with his own name, Farida, as if he's tapping himself on the shoulder. One, on Ang 1381, in paraphrase: rise, Farid, make your ablutions and offer your morning prayer. The head that doesn't bow to the Master, cut it off and set it aside. That's the language of a Sufi's day: wudu, the washing before prayer, and namaz, the prayer itself. And it's blunt. A head that won't bow isn't worth carrying. Farid isn't threatening anyone. He's saying that a life without bowing is missing its point. Now the other salok, from the same pages, and it's the honest one. In paraphrase: the dervish's door is a hard path, and I walk the way the world walks. I've tied up a bundle and lifted it onto my head; where can I go and throw it down? A dervish is a Sufi who has given up the world. Farid, a revered Sufi, admits he's carrying a bundle he can't put down. Hold those two together. Get up and bow; and this is hard, and I'm not there. Some readers hear in that why the Gurus kept his words. He doesn't pretend. He speaks in Punjabi, the speech a farmer or a weaver could follow. And there's a quiet gift on the page: a Muslim's reminder to rise for morning prayer sits in the Sikh scripture, kept and sung, in his own words. Farid's verses belong to Sikh devotion, and Farid remains a Sufi of the Punjab.
screen: `FARIDA — TAPPING HIMSELF ON THE SHOULDER.` · `RISE, WASH, AND BOW.` · `THE DERVISH'S DOOR IS HARD.` · `A BUNDLE HE CAN'T PUT DOWN.` · then, large: `THE SUFI OF PUNJAB.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: sit still like a Sufi. If you can, wash your hands and face first, slowly, as a way of arriving. Then sit, and let your head bow a little, the chin dropping toward the chest. Stay there, still. When the mind wanders to its bundle, the list, the worry, just notice it's on your head, and bow again. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out. The bell holds the time.
Sheikh Farid of Pakpattan. A Chishti Sufi of the Punjab, who calls himself to prayer and admits the way is hard, in verses kept in the Granth.
Your line: the sufi of punjab. Today, once, before something begins, a meal, a meeting, wash your hands slowly and bow your head for one breath. Day seven hundred sixty-one.

762.title: Love from the heart
762.hook: they are true who love the Lord from the heart; those with one thing in the heart and another on the lips are false (Asa, Farid, ang 488)
762.howItsDone: Farid's hymns in Raag Asa are sung in kirtan in gurdwaras, and Sikhs read this line alongside the Gurus' own teaching that the tongue should speak what is truly in the mind.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Sheikh Farid of Pakpattan: rise, wash and bow, and admit the way is hard. Your line was the sufi of punjab. Did you bow your head for one breath? Day seven hundred sixty-two.

A card goes around the office for someone's birthday. A page full of signatures, nearly all saying the same thing: have a great one. One of them is from the person who complained about her all week. The handwriting is just as cheerful as the rest. Nobody can tell from the card. That gap, between what's written on the outside and what's going on inside, is exactly where Farid puts his finger in one of his hymns. Today: love from the heart.
screen: `A CARD FULL OF SIGNATURES.` → `THE SAME CHEERFUL HANDWRITING.` → `WHAT'S INSIDE?`

segments.voice: Farid's hymns in the Guru Granth Sahib aren't only short saloks. A few are longer shabads set to raag, sung like the Gurus' own. This one is in Raag Asa, on Ang 488, and it opens with a line that's simple to say and hard to live. In paraphrase: those who love the Lord from the heart are the true ones. Those who have one thing in the heart and another on the lips are counted false. Notice the words he chooses: dil, the heart, and muhabbat, love. It's the Sufi's language of love for the Beloved. Then he paints the two kinds of people side by side. In paraphrase again: those dyed in the love of the Lord are delighted by the sight of Him. Those who forget the Name are a burden on the earth. Dyed is the picture. Cloth that's dyed doesn't have color painted on top; the color goes all the way through the thread. So the true one isn't the one with the loudest prayer. It's the one whose love goes all the way through, so the inside and the outside are the same color. And Farid isn't pointing at hypocrites in the street. The hymn holds a mirror. It's easy to say a warm thing with a cool heart, or to sign the card. The line doesn't ask for more words. It asks the words and the heart to match. And for Sikhs this joins the Gurus' own teaching, that what is on the tongue should be what is in the mind. A Sufi's line, at home in the Sikh scripture.
screen: `A SHABAD IN RAAG ASA, ANG 488.` · `ONE THING IN THE HEART, ANOTHER ON THE LIPS.` · `DYED ALL THE WAY THROUGH.` · `NOT MORE WORDS: MATCHING WORDS.` · then, large: `THE HEART AND THE LIPS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: say what you mean. In the sit, think back over the last day for one thing you said that didn't match what was inside. A yes you didn't mean, a fine that wasn't fine, a compliment with a cool heart behind it. Don't punish yourself. Just look at the gap. Then find the true sentence underneath it, said kindly. Hold it until it's ready to say. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out. The bell holds the time.
Love from the heart. Farid's line in Raag Asa: the true ones love the Lord from the heart, and their lips say the same thing.
Your line: the heart and the lips. Today, once, before you answer someone, check that the heart and the lips agree, and then speak. Day seven hundred sixty-two.

original.note: Gurmukhi: the heart; Farid's hymn opens with love from the dil.

trapdoor: what you thought: a line about being sincere.

763.title: Look under your own collar
763.hook: if you are wise, don't write black marks against others; look within your own collar (Farid salok, ang 1378)
763.howItsDone: Farid's saloks are read and sung in gurdwaras with the rest of the Guru Granth Sahib, and Sikhs read this couplet as a reminder to examine oneself before judging others.

segments.voice: Yesterday, love from the heart: one thing inside and another on the lips is counted false. Your line was the heart and the lips. Did they agree when you spoke? Day seven hundred sixty-three.

A red pen is a satisfying thing to hold. Circle the typo. Strike the wrong figure. Put a mark in the margin and a note beside it. Some minds are very good at this, and not only with paper: they keep a running ledger of other people's mistakes, neat and up to date. Farid has a couplet for the person holding that pen. We touched it earlier this year, when his verses came into the Guru's keeping. Today we stay with it, because it ends the week. Today: look under your own collar.
screen: `A RED PEN IN HAND.` → `A LEDGER OF OTHER PEOPLE'S MISTAKES.` → `FARID'S COUPLET FOR THE PEN.`

segments.voice: Here it is, on Ang 1378, in paraphrase: Farid, if you have a keen and subtle mind, don't write black marks against anyone else. Bow your head and look within your own collar. Three things are packed into that. First, who it's addressed to. Not the fool. The clever one. Some readers hear in this that sharpness is exactly what makes a person good at spotting other people's faults. The gift and the danger are the same tool. Second, the black marks. The picture is writing: an account book, a record kept against someone. Farid doesn't say the faults aren't real. He says don't be the one keeping the book. Third, the collar. The opening of a shirt at the neck. To see inside it, you have to bow your head, which is the posture of prayer, the posture Farid called himself to at dawn. So looking at yourself honestly and bowing turn out to be one movement. Now look back over this week, because it has been circling this idea. Kabir spoke his hymns to Loi, at home, where words have to be true. He went to Maghar, because the place doesn't save you. His saloks were short and sharp, and he was blunt with pride and humble before everyone else. Then Farid: rising to pray and admitting the way is hard, and asking that the heart and the lips agree. Every one of those turns the eyes inward. The collar is the plainest picture of all. Before the red pen moves, the head bows.
screen: `THE KEEN AND SUBTLE MIND.` · `DON'T KEEP THE BLACK BOOK.` · `BOW TO SEE INSIDE YOUR COLLAR.` · `A WEEK OF TURNING THE EYES INWARD.` · then, large: `LOOK WITHIN YOUR COLLAR.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: check yourself before judging. In the sit, let someone you've been marking come to mind, at work, online, at home. Notice the fault you've written down for them. Then bow your head a little, physically, and ask one plain question: where does that same thing show up in me? Don't rush the answer. Just look inside the collar. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out. The bell holds the time.
Look under your own collar. Farid's couplet for the clever mind: don't write black marks against others; bow, and look within.
screen: `LOOK UNDER YOUR OWN COLLAR — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: look within your collar. Today, the next time the red pen comes out in your head, bow first, and look there before you mark anyone. Day seven hundred sixty-three.

screen: `DAY 763 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: DRY BREAD AND COOL WATER.`
